title: Sink or Float?
subject: science
learningGoal: Predict and test whether objects sink or float, and notice it isn't only about size.
realWorldHook: Huge ships float while a tiny coin sinks. How can that be?

materials.item: A tub or sink of water
5 household objects (spoon, apple, cork, crayon, lid)
materials.householdSubstitution: Anything waterproof: plastic toys, a sponge, a key

noPurchaseRoute: Use a bowl of water and any five waterproof things you already have.
parentPreview: Your child sorts objects into 'sink' or 'float' predictions, tests each one, and notices surprises, like a big apple floating and a small key sinking.

parent.parentSays: A huge ship floats but a tiny pebble sinks. Strange! Let's investigate.

child.screen: Big ships float. Tiny pebbles sink. Let's find out why!
child.readAloudText: Big ships float. Tiny pebbles sink. Let's investigate.

parent.parentSays: Sort the objects into two piles: 'I think it will sink' and 'I think it will float'.
parent.whyThisWorks: Predicting first makes the test meaningful. Surprises are the best part.

child.screen: Sort: sink pile or float pile?
child.readAloudText: Make a sink pile and a float pile.

parent.parentSays: Gently place each object in the water. Did it do what you predicted?

child.screen: Test each one gently. Did it sink or float?
child.readAloudText: Put each one in the water gently. Watch closely.

parent.parentSays: Ask what happened to the apple. Many children expect it to sink.
Was anything a surprise? Why do you think it floated or sank?

child.readAloudText: Which one surprised you? Tell your grown-up why.

parent.parentSays: Ask the two check questions below. Give your child time to think, then note how each one went.
What would you like to test next time?

expectedResponses: Notices big things can float and small things can sink

misconceptions.signal: Thinks big or heavy-looking things always sink.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: The apple is bigger than the key. Which one floated?

misconceptions.signal: Drops objects from a height so they splash under and look like they sink.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: If we place it gently, does it do the same thing?

checkQuestions.parentAsks: Does a big object always sink?

interpretation.clear: Says no, with an example from the test.

checkQuestions.parentAsks: Why do you think boats are hollow inside?

interpretation.partial: Has a guess about air or shape.

child.readAloudText: Why are boats hollow inside? Tell your grown-up your idea.

extension: Make a foil boat. How many coins or blocks can it carry before it sinks?
accessibilityAdaptations: Use a deep tray at table height.
Use bigger objects that are easy to grip.

hazards: Spilled water can make floors slippery
Small objects can be a choking hazard
safety.supervision: An adult stays within arm's reach the whole time. Use a shallow tub on a towel. Coins and other small items are a choking hazard. Keep them away from younger siblings and use larger counters (blocks, bottle caps glued in pairs, or folded paper squares) if anyone in the room is under 3.
stopConditions: Water spills on the floor (stop and dry it first)
Anyone puts an object in their mouth
A child leans over or into the water
safety.cleanup: Empty the water into a sink or plants, dry the objects and wipe the floor.
